title: BIA Rules Returned Hearing Notice No Longer Blocks Removal Order
excerpt: In Matter of Chamorro Castillo, decided October 22, the Board held that a notice mailed to the only address on file can support an in absentia removal order even when it comes back undeliverable.
body:
• The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled on October 22 in Matter of Chamorro Castillo, 30 I&N Dec. 170 (BIA 2026), that a hearing notice mailed to the only address in the record can support a removal order even if it comes back undeliverable.
  • EOIR recorded 311,130 in absentia removal orders in fiscal 2025 and 281,867 in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, up from 34,330 in fiscal 2016.
  • Reader action: if you move while a case is pending, file Form EOIR-33 with your immigration court within five working days - telling USCIS or ICE alone does not update the court, and a full mailbox or returned envelope will not by itself reopen your case.
  • The Board rejected the argument that a judge should have phoned the number on the respondent's Form I-830, holding courts are quasi-judicial bodies, not investigators.

A returned envelope is no longer enough to undo a deportation order entered in a person's absence. In Matter of Chamorro Castillo, decided October 22, the Board of Immigration Appeals held that when a hearing notice mailed to the only address in the record comes back undeliverable, there are no further reasonable steps a court or the Board can take, so an in absentia removal order based on that mailing can stand. The precedent, listed by the Executive Office for Immigration Review among its Volume 30 decisions, binds immigration judges nationwide.

A full mailbox and a phone number nobody called

The respondent was released from detention in 2019, and DHS told the court his address on ICE Form I-830, which also listed a phone number. The court mailed his hearing notice there; it came back marked unable to forward. He missed the January 2020 hearing and was ordered removed. On his motion to reopen, his own documents confirmed the address was correct, and a postal letter explained his mailbox had been full, so the mail was held 10 days and returned as unclaimed, according to Immigration Analytics' account of the decision.

The Ninth Circuit sent the case back in January 2026 to apply United States v. Rivera-Valdes (2025), built on Jones v. Flowers: notice fails when the government knows service was ineffective and takes no reasonably available extra steps. The respondent argued the judge could have called the number on the I-830.

"The court mailed the hearing notice to the respondent's correct address, and there was no other address in the record."

- Board of Immigration Appeals, Matter of Chamorro Castillo

Chief Appellate Immigration Judge Garry Malphrus, for a three-member panel, rejected that argument. Courts are quasi-judicial bodies, not investigators, the Board reasoned: respondents must report address changes on Form EOIR-33, and DHS must report a released respondent's address on Form I-830. Phoning a respondent would raise ex parte contact, identity verification and confidentiality problems under 8 U.S.C. 1367.

What the ruling does and does not decide

The holding is narrower than its headline. The Board distinguished Rivera-Valdes, where the notice went to an address missing Ave., and Meza Medina v. Blanche, where the address came from a third party. Here the address was right. The Board also said it is appropriate for DHS to tell the courts when it learns of a different address - leaving a path for a respondent who can show DHS had a newer address, from a USCIS filing or an ICE check-in, and never passed it along. That case is not decided here.

The scale of in absentia orders

EOIR statistics cited in the analysis show 311,130 in absentia orders in fiscal 2025 and 281,867 in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, against 34,330 in fiscal 2016. Orders against people released from custody reached 17,565 through the third quarter of fiscal 2026, already above the 16,003 for all of fiscal 2025. For them, the I-830 address at release may be the only address the court ever has.

What this means if you have a pending case

EOIR instructs respondents to report any change of address within five working days, using Form EOIR-33/IC for a court case or EOIR-33/BIA for a Board appeal, filed separately for each family member. Read the official list of precedent decisions, including Matter of Chamorro Castillo in EOIR's Virtual Law Library, and follow EOIR's instructions to update your address with the immigration court online through Respondent Access, in person or by mail. Updating USCIS or ICE does not update the court.

What happens next

The ruling applies to pending cases and motions to reopen now. It can be tested by a petition for review in the Ninth Circuit, whose rulings set the test the Board applied; because the question is constitutional, that court will decide it for itself. This article is general information, not legal advice.
